title: As Wisconsin cities flee Flock, its shared camera network loses value
gist: A wave of Wisconsin cities are canceling contracts with license-plate-camera firm Flock over privacy concerns, and because Flock's value derives from cross-jurisdiction data sharing, each departure makes the network less useful to remaining users—a reverse network effect, with some cities switching to Axon.

insights.claim: Because much of Flock's value comes from access to cameras in other jurisdictions, each city that leaves makes the network less useful, triggering further cancellations—McFarland dropped its plan citing a shrinking Dane County database and Kaukauna cited the inability to partner with area communities.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Demonstrates network effects can run backward for surveillance/data platforms—a cascading-churn risk investors should weigh for Flock's model.
insights.quote: The same “network effect” that helps build a business can also work in the other direction once customers start to flee.

insights.claim: Dane County (including Madison) cut $80,000 in Flock funding and banned further expenditures in April, cutting off its data from 140 other law enforcement agencies across multiple states.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Quantifies how one large customer's exit degrades the shared network for many downstream agencies.

insights.claim: Multiple Wisconsin cities cited Fourth Amendment and privacy concerns in leaving Flock, with the broad backlash pushing Flock to announce mandatory new audit controls and lower default data retention periods for US users.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Public privacy pressure is directly forcing product/policy changes—regulatory and reputational risk for the surveillance-tech sector.

insights.claim: Cities are not abandoning license-plate readers entirely but switching vendors, with Grand Chute moving to Axon and UW-Madison police seeking an alternative ALPR vendor.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Demand for ALPR persists; the churn is a competitive-share shift (notably to Axon) rather than sector collapse.
